stem: A model includes `CASE WHEN minimum_nights = 0 THEN 1 ELSE minimum_nights END AS minimum_nights`, and a custom generic test checks that `minimum_nights` is positive. The raw source column sometimes contains `0`. The team needs to know exactly which values this test actually evaluates: the raw source's `0`s, or something else. What does the test see?

option_texts.A: The materialized column's post-CASE values, where every former `0` has already become `1`, so the test never observes a `0`
option_texts.B: Both the raw `0` values and the transformed `1` values, since dbt tests against the full lineage, not just the final table
option_texts.C: Only the raw source's `0` values, since a generic test always queries the source directly, bypassing the model's SQL
option_texts.D: The test fails deterministically, because testing a derived column that uses a CASE expression is not supported

drill_answer_short: A test queries the model's materialized output, which already reflects any CASE transformation
decision_hinge: Data tests return a set of failing records. Generic data tests are select statements that seek to grab failing records from the model, evaluating whatever that model's query actually produces.

plausible_options.B: The raw source column sometimes contains `0`

eliminated_by.C: The raw source column sometimes contains `0`
eliminated_by.D: a custom generic test checks that `minimum_nights` is positive

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a generic test queries the model's own output relation, it does not separately scan raw source data too
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a test attached to a model's column queries that model's materialized output, not the raw source directly
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt places no restriction on testing a column derived from a CASE expression

stem: A dimension model casts a raw `price` column with `REPLACE(price_str, '$') :: NUMBER(10, 2) AS price`, and the raw source occasionally has a non-numeric value like `"N/A"`. A `not_null` test is attached to the resulting `price` column. The team needs to know what actually happens on the next `dbt build`, given that the cast itself cannot succeed on that row. What's the real outcome?

option_texts.A: The model fails to build with a Database Error during SQL execution, because the warehouse rejects the invalid cast before the model even finishes materializing
option_texts.B: The model builds successfully, and the `not_null` test then catches the bad row as a null value
option_texts.C: The cast silently produces `NULL` for the unparseable value, and the model builds, but the test is never actually evaluated
option_texts.D: dbt detects the cast risk at parse time and refuses to compile the model at all

drill_answer_short: An invalid cast is a Database Error during the model's own build, which happens before any test can even run
decision_hinge: SQL execution: run the models -- Database Error. Database Errors come from your data warehouse, and dbt passes the message on. Tests run after a model has already been built.

plausible_options.C: the raw source occasionally has a non-numeric value like `"N/A"`

B.signal: the raw source occasionally has a non-numeric value like `"N/A"`
B.requires_fact: SQL execution produces a Database Error when the warehouse rejects a query; a model must finish building successfully before any of its tests can run against it.

eliminated_by.D: the raw source occasionally has a non-numeric value like `"N/A"`

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — an invalid cast fails the build itself, so the model never reaches a state where its test can run
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — some warehouses do coerce a bad cast to NULL, but the scenario as a NUMBER cast on non-numeric text typically fails the query outright, which is the documented Database Error path
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt's parsing stage checks Jinja and YAML validity, not runtime cast safety against real data

stem: An incremental model's SQL has `{% if is_incremental() %} {% if var("start_date", False) and var("end_date", False) %} {{ log('Loading incrementally', info=True) }} {% endif %} {% endif %}`. The team runs a normal incremental build with no `--vars` passed at all. The team needs to know whether the log line prints to the terminal. Does it, and why?

option_texts.A: No, because `var("start_date", False)` defaults to `False` when no `--vars` are passed, so the inner `if` never evaluates true
option_texts.B: Yes, because `is_incremental()` being true is the only condition that matters for this log line
option_texts.C: No, because `log(..., info=True)` only ever writes to the log file, never to stdout, regardless of the surrounding conditionals
option_texts.D: Yes, because `var("start_date", False)` always falls back to a project-level `vars:` default even when no `--vars` are passed on the command line

drill_answer_short: var() with a default of False returns False when no --vars are passed, so the nested if is never true
decision_hinge: The var() function returns the value defined in your project or passed using --vars, based on precedence. You can provide a default value as a second argument.

plausible_options.D: The team runs a normal incremental build with no `--vars` passed at all

eliminated_by.B: runs a normal incremental build with no `--vars` passed at all

C.signal: The team needs to know whether the log line prints to the terminal
C.requires_fact: log() takes an info argument: if False, write to the log file; if True, write to both the log file and stdout.

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — the log line is nested inside a second if that also must evaluate true
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — info=True does write to stdout, but only if the log() call is actually reached, which this scenario prevents
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — var() does fall back to a project vars: default when one exists, but the stem never says one is set here

stem: A hosts model uses `NVL(host_name, 'Anonymous') AS host_name`, and a `not_null` test is applied to `host_name`. The raw source data has NULL values in its `host_name` column for some rows. The team needs to predict whether the `not_null` test passes or fails. What happens, and why?

option_texts.A: The test passes, because `NVL` replaces every NULL with a placeholder string before the column is materialized, so the test never sees a NULL
option_texts.B: The test fails, because `not_null` always checks the raw source column regardless of any transformation applied downstream
option_texts.C: The test passes only for rows where the source value was not NULL, and silently skips the rest
option_texts.D: The test's result is undefined, since `not_null` cannot be combined with a model that uses `NVL`

drill_answer_short: NVL replaces NULLs before materialization, so a not_null test on the resulting column passes
decision_hinge: not_null: the column should not contain null values. If the data test returns zero failing rows, it passes, and your assertion has been validated.

plausible_options.B: The raw source data has NULL values in its `host_name` column for some rows

eliminated_by.C: The team needs to predict whether the `not_null` test passes or fails
eliminated_by.D: The team needs to predict whether the `not_null` test passes or fails

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a generic test queries the model's materialized output, not the untransformed raw source
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a data test has no partial-pass behavior; it either returns zero failing rows or it doesn't
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — not_null has no documented incompatibility with any particular SQL function used upstream

stem: An incremental reviews model needs to handle late-arriving reviews, up to 48 hours late, and deduplicate reviews that share the same surrogate key. The team needs the TWO configuration choices that genuinely address both requirements together. Which TWO are correct?

option_texts.A: Use `incremental_strategy='merge'` so a matching key updates the existing row instead of inserting a duplicate
option_texts.B: Set `unique_key` to the review's key column, so merge has something to match existing rows against
option_texts.C: Use `incremental_strategy='append'`, since append is the simplest strategy for any time-series data
option_texts.D: Omit `unique_key` entirely, since merge always deduplicates automatically regardless of configuration

drill_answer_short: merge with a configured unique_key both updates existing rows and prevents duplicate inserts
decision_hinge: merge inserts records with a unique_key that do not exist yet in the destination table and updates records with keys that do exist. merge without a unique_key behaves like the append strategy.

plausible_options.C: needs to handle late-arriving reviews, up to 48 hours late, and deduplicate reviews that share the same surrogate key

D.signal: needs to handle late-arriving reviews, up to 48 hours late, and deduplicate reviews that share the same surrogate key
D.requires_fact: merge without a unique_key behaves like the append strategy, so a unique_key must actually be configured for deduplication to occur.

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — append is a real, simpler strategy, but it never updates existing rows or deduplicates, which this scenario requires
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — merge does not deduplicate automatically without a configured unique_key

option_texts.B: `source('seeds', 'full_moon_dates')`, since a CSV file is raw data dbt did not build
option_texts.C: `seed('full_moon_dates')`, a dedicated Jinja function reserved for referencing seeds specifically
option_texts.D: A raw table name with no Jinja function, since seeds bypass dbt's dependency tracking entirely

drill_answer_short: A seed is referenced with ref(), the same as a model, once it has been loaded by dbt seed
decision_hinge: This refers to the table created from seeds/country_codes.csv: select * from {{ ref('country_codes') }}.

plausible_options.B: `full_moon_dates`, a seed loaded from a CSV

eliminated_by.C: needs the correct Jinja function to pull this seed into the mart's SQL
eliminated_by.D: needs the correct Jinja function to pull this seed into the mart's SQL

distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — seeds fully participate in dbt's dependency graph like any other resource

stem: A team wants to add a scoring model that uses pandas and scikit-learn, both present on the warehouse's Python environment. They need the approach dbt documents for this, rather than working around the limitation of SQL-only models. Which approach is correct?

option_texts.A: Write a native dbt Python model whose `model()` function uses pandas and third-party packages like scikit-learn directly, as long as they're installed and available to the platform's Python runtime
option_texts.B: Write the scoring logic as a Jinja macro that calls out to Python via `run_query()`, since dbt SQL models cannot call pandas or scikit-learn
option_texts.C: Write the logic in a `{% docs %}` block, since Python code can only be embedded there, not in a model file
option_texts.D: This is not possible in dbt Core at all; dbt Python models only support the built-in DataFrame API, never third-party packages

drill_answer_short: A dbt Python model can call third-party packages like scikit-learn if they're installed on the platform runtime
decision_hinge: You can define functions that depend on third-party packages so long as those packages are installed and available to the Python runtime on your data platform.

plausible_options.B: both present on the warehouse's Python environment

eliminated_by.C: They need the approach dbt documents for this, rather than working around the limitation of SQL-only models

D.signal: both present on the warehouse's Python environment
D.requires_fact: You can define functions that depend on third-party packages so long as those packages are installed and available to the Python runtime on your data platform.

distractor_traps.B: T7: over-engineering — dbt Python models support this natively; a macro-based run_query() workaround is unnecessary
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — docs blocks hold markdown documentation, not executable Python code
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — dbt Python models explicitly support third-party packages when the platform runtime has them installed

stem: A developer iterating on a chain of marts runs `dbt run --select +fct_sessions --sample="1 day"`, finishing in 90 seconds instead of the usual 18 minutes. Before trusting the result as a full validation, the team needs to know exactly what `--sample` actually filtered, and whether every model in the chain was actually sampled. What's true about this run?

option_texts.A: `--sample` applies time-based filtering, and models without a configured `event_time` are not scoped down by it at all
option_texts.B: `--sample` randomly selects 1 day's worth of rows from each table, regardless of any time column configuration
option_texts.C: `--sample` only limits the very first model in the selection; every downstream model still processes its full historical volume
option_texts.D: `--sample` behaves identically to `--empty`, returning zero rows for every selected and upstream model

drill_answer_short: --sample does time-based filtering; models without event_time configured are not filtered
decision_hinge: The --sample flag will become more robust over time, but it only supports time-based sampling for now. Since it's using time-based sampling, you need to set event_time for the relevant models.

plausible_options.C: finishing in 90 seconds instead of the usual 18 minutes

eliminated_by.B: finishing in 90 seconds instead of the usual 18 minutes

D.signal: finishing in 90 seconds instead of the usual 18 minutes
D.requires_fact: Sample mode takes the --empty flag's validation a step further by including a sampling of data from the model(s) in your development schema; --empty itself returns zero rows, which --sample explicitly goes beyond.

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — --sample is explicitly documented as time-based, not a random row sample
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — --sample scopes to nodes with event_time configured throughout the selection, not only the first model
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — --sample is documented as going beyond --empty's zero-row validation by including real sampled data
